title: Department of Orthographic Mutations
subtitle: Twelve small failures of language that learned to reproduce
curatorial_thesis: Internet language does not merely carry memes. Punctuation, spelling, syntax, capitalization, and error can become the meme's transmissible body.
registration_note: OM numbers are working collection identifiers, not permanent M## register IDs. A record receives an M## ID only after a separate rights, provenance, and curatorial review.

display_policy.rule: Render the linguistic mechanism as original typography, diagrams, or interface-like notation. Do not reproduce a source meme image, copyrighted character, screenshot, logo, or identifiable person.
display_policy.rights_note: Descriptive titles and linked research sources identify the forms under discussion; they do not authorize reproduction of the best-known visual instance.

specimens.title: Punctuation Saves Lives
specimens.mechanism: A mark changes the grammatical relationship between an action and its apparent object.
specimens.mutation: The comma migrates; kinship becomes cuisine.
specimens.epitaph: One breath between invitation and ingestion.
specimens.curatorial_note: The familiar formula turns proofreading into miniature catastrophe. Its durability comes from compression: one tiny mark, one instantly legible reversal, no picture required.
specimens.source_label: Open English at SLCC — Punctuation Memes and Choice
specimens.rights_posture: Original typographic demonstration; no circulating meme image reproduced.

specimens.title: Oxford Comma Wars
specimens.mechanism: An optional serial comma becomes a proxy contest over clarity, authority, and house style.
specimens.epitaph: The smallest battlefield in the style guide.
specimens.curatorial_note: The meme is not simply about ambiguity. It lets people perform an editorial identity in public, turning a convention into a badge of belonging.
specimens.rights_posture: Original list and typographic treatment; no source cartoon or image macro reproduced.

specimens.title: A Lot / Alot
specimens.mechanism: A common word-boundary error is reimagined as if the fused form named a thing.
specimens.mutation: Whitespace disappears; an imaginary noun appears.
specimens.epitaph: The space went missing. Something moved in.
specimens.curatorial_note: Allie Brosh’s famous ‘Alot’ gives a spelling correction a body and personality. This exhibit keeps only the linguistic mutation: two words, the gap between them, and the creature we refuse to redraw.
specimens.rights_posture: Text-only analysis. Allie Brosh’s character and artwork are not reproduced or imitated.

specimens.title: Muphry’s Law
specimens.mechanism: A criticism of another person’s writing attracts an error of its own.
specimens.curatorial_note: Often grouped with Skitt’s Law online, the form punishes certainty rather than error. The higher the corrective posture, the more memorable the returning typo.
specimens.rights_posture: Original wording and diagram; no source post or screenshot reproduced.

specimens.title: Typoglycemia
specimens.mechanism: Interior letters are transposed while enough lexical and sentence context remains to support recognition.
specimens.mutation: A conditional reading effect becomes a universal neuroscience claim.
specimens.epitaph: Readable is not the same as proven.
specimens.curatorial_note: The circulating paragraph is a double specimen: a genuine demonstration of flexible word recognition and a false attribution to Cambridge research. The debunking travels more slowly than the wonder.
specimens.rights_posture: New scrambled phrase; the widely copied email paragraph is not reproduced.

specimens.title: The OUGH Outbreak
specimens.mechanism: The same four-letter sequence carries multiple pronunciations across common English words.
specimens.curatorial_note: Lists of -ough words turn the historical sediment of English spelling into spectacle. They are less a lesson than a public demonstration that the system contains fossils.
specimens.source_label: British Council IELTS — confusing English words

specimens.title: TEH
specimens.mechanism: A frequent keyboard transposition stops functioning only as error and begins functioning as tone.
specimens.epitaph: The typo learned when to arrive on purpose.
specimens.curatorial_note: ‘Teh’ crosses the decisive boundary from mistake to selectable voice. Once intentional, it can signal speed, irony, in-group fluency, or affectionate incompetence.
specimens.rights_posture: Original keyboard diagram; no source screenshot reproduced.

specimens.title: The !1 Phenomenon
specimens.mechanism: A stray numeral reveals the physical release of Shift during an escalating run of exclamation marks.
specimens.curatorial_note: The 1 is funny because it records the hand. Later, deliberate forms such as ‘!!1one’ imitate the accident and make excess itself visible.
specimens.rights_posture: Original typographic treatment; no source post reproduced.

specimens.title: I Accidentally the Whole Thing
specimens.mechanism: A required verb is omitted, leaving the listener to infer an event from context and comic panic.
specimens.mutation: The grammatical hole becomes the punchline.
specimens.epitaph: The verb did not survive transmission.
specimens.curatorial_note: Unlike a simple typo, the missing word opens a generative slot. Each repetition can imply a different disaster while keeping the same conspicuous absence.
specimens.rights_posture: Original sentence and missing-word notation; no source image reproduced.

specimens.title: LOLspeak
specimens.mechanism: Nonstandard spelling, altered auxiliaries, lexical play, and cat-centred voice combine into a repeatable grammar.
specimens.mutation: A caption style becomes a language game.
specimens.epitaph: The cat is optional. The syntax remains infected.
specimens.curatorial_note: LOLspeak is important because it became productive: participants did not merely repeat one caption, but generated new sentences within a recognizable rule-set. The museum studies that rule-set without displaying a cat photograph.
specimens.rights_posture: Original grammatical diagram. No cat photograph, LOLcat image macro, or third-party caption reproduced.

specimens.title: Dogespeak
specimens.mechanism: Degree modifiers are paired with grammatically unexpected words in short, floating fragments.
specimens.mutation: Incorrect combination becomes a generative rule.
specimens.epitaph: Much grammar. Very mutation. Still alive.
specimens.curatorial_note: Doge’s visual source is registered elsewhere as M01 and declined for display. Here the language stands alone: brief fragments, deliberate mismatch, and a voice recognizable after the photograph is gone.
specimens.rights_posture: Original typographic analysis; Kabosu’s photograph and Doge artwork are not reproduced.

specimens.title: Alternating-Capital Sarcasm
specimens.mechanism: Irregular upper- and lowercase letters make a written sentence perform a mocking vocal contour.
specimens.epitaph: Prosody entered through the Shift key.
specimens.curatorial_note: The convention became larger than its best-known SpongeBob template. Alternating case can now carry mockery without any image, a rare example of a meme’s caption escaping its original visual host.
specimens.rights_posture: Original sentence and typography. SpongeBob character art and source imagery are not reproduced or imitated.

writers_at_work.note: These are original museum observations about recurring writing-meme motifs, not claims that one canonical image or phrasing owns the joke.
